ego.name: Joseph Weizenbaum
ego.summary: Joseph Weizenbaum was a German-American computer scientist, MIT professor, and critic of technological determinism. He created ELIZA, an early conversational computer program, and later argued that moral judgment and consequential decisions must remain human responsibilities.

connections.relationship_description: Weizenbaum's father was a master furrier. Joseph emigrated with him and the rest of their Jewish family from Germany to the United States in 1936.
connections.notes: The family left Germany after Nazi persecution affected Joseph's schooling.

connections.relationship_description: Henriette Weizenbaum was Joseph's mother. She left Bremen for the United States with Joseph, Jechiel Weizenbaum, and their Jewish family in 1936.
connections.notes: The family left Germany after Nazi persecution forced Joseph out of his Berlin secondary school.

connections.relationship_description: Ruth was Weizenbaum's wife; together they had four daughters.
connections.notes: The family later lived in Berlin, where Weizenbaum returned in 1996.

connections.relationship_description: Heinrich Weizenbaum was Joseph Weizenbaum's brother and also became a computer scientist, later using the name Henry F. Sherwood after becoming a United States citizen.
connections.notes: The article identifies Heinrich as one of Joseph's brothers.

connections.relationship_description: Yarbrough coauthored the 1964 Communications of the ACM publication SLIP with Weizenbaum, concerning his list-processing language.
connections.notes: Their 1964 collaboration concerned Weizenbaum's SLIP list-processing language.

connections.relationship_description: Bobrow and Weizenbaum coauthored the 1964 paper List Processing and Extension of Language Facility by Embedding.
connections.notes: Their work concerned list processing and programming-language facilities during Weizenbaum's early MIT period.

connections.relationship_description: Hagopian coauthored the 1958 paper The GE-100 Data Processing System with Weizenbaum and other General Electric colleagues.
connections.notes: The publication arose from Weizenbaum's systems-engineering work at General Electric's Computer Development Laboratory.

connections.relationship_description: McCarthy and Weizenbaum appeared with Benjamin Kuipers in a 1976 SIGART Newsletter discussion, Computer Power and Human Reason, engaging questions raised by Weizenbaum's critique of computing and artificial intelligence.
connections.notes: Their 1976 SIGART Newsletter discussion addressed questions raised by Computer Power and Human Reason.

connections.relationship_description: Weizenbaum wrote A Response to Donald Michie, a 1977 book review in the International Journal of Man-Machine Studies, in the context of their disagreement over artificial intelligence.
connections.notes: Weizenbaum's 1977 response to Michie followed their published disagreement about artificial intelligence.

connections.relationship_description: Wendt coauthored Wo sind sie, die Inseln der Vernunft im Cyberstrom? with Weizenbaum in 2006; an English edition, Islands in the Cyberstream, was published after his death.
connections.notes: Their 2006 book addressed technology, reason, and social responsibility.

connections.relationship_description: Akbar coauthored Vom Handeln im Netz: Dimensionen der Globalisierung with Weizenbaum and Anne Helfensteller, published in 2002.
connections.notes: Their 2002 book addressed action in a networked and globalized society.

connections.relationship_description: Helfensteller coauthored Vom Handeln im Netz: Dimensionen der Globalisierung with Weizenbaum and Omar Akbar, published in 2002.
connections.notes: Their 2002 book addressed the social dimensions of digital networks.

connections.relationship_description: Kurzweil and Weizenbaum appeared as contrasting voices on artificial intelligence and technological futures in Jens Schanze's documentary Plug & Pray, filmed with Weizenbaum before his 2008 death and released in 2010.
connections.notes: Plug & Pray presents Weizenbaum and Kurzweil as contrasting voices on artificial intelligence and technological futures.

connections.relationship_description: Schanze made the documentary Plug & Pray, in which Weizenbaum was a central figure and commented on the promises and consequences of artificial intelligence and computer technology.
connections.notes: Filming with Weizenbaum continued until shortly before his death in March 2008.

connections.relationship_description: Kuipers participated with Weizenbaum and John McCarthy in the 1976 SIGART Newsletter discussion Computer Power and Human Reason.
connections.notes: The documented connection is their joint published discussion of computing's human and social consequences.

category_summaries.summary: Weizenbaum's parents took their Jewish family out of Nazi Germany in 1936. The move made his education in Detroit possible. His brother Heinrich also entered computing, and his wife Ruth and their four daughters formed his later family life. After 1996, Weizenbaum lived in Berlin near one of his daughters and his parents' former apartment.

Weizenbaum's academic circle included collaborators and critics working on artificial intelligence and its social consequences. His 1976 book Computer Power and Human Reason led to published exchanges with figures such as John McCarthy, Benjamin Kuipers, and Donald Michie. Later collaborations extended his writing to globalization, digital networks, and scientific responsibility.

Weizenbaum's technical collaborators span his work at General Electric and MIT. Work on the GE-100 system, SLIP, and language facilities gave him practical experience with large computers and symbolic programming. ELIZA grew from this period of hands-on computing research.

Documentary film brought Weizenbaum's arguments about computers and artificial intelligence to wider audiences. In Plug & Pray, Jens Schanze filmed Weizenbaum alongside other voices on technology's promises and consequences.
